context: Since we will often have to extend an embedding with a value for a new position, we define µ + (i 7→ α) as the mapping µ0 such that µ0 (i) = α, µ0 (k) = µ(k) for k < i and µ0 (k + 1) = µ(k) for k ≥ i in the domain of µ. A full proof is given in Appendix B, and we cover here only a few key cases. Consider first an application of (`G) with Γ ` ∆, G ϕ at position i, when C 0 ; H2 is empty. For any βi < µ(i) there exists γi with βi ≤ γi < µ(i) such that M, γi 6|= H(i), hence there also exists γi0 > γi such that M, γi0 6|= ϕ. Let γ be the least ordinal that contains all such γi0 . We have that µ(i) ≤ γ. If µ(i) = γ, then µ(i) must be a limit ordinal. Hence C 6= ? and the third premise H30 is available. We construct a counter-model (M, µ0 ) for it by taking µ0 = µ + (k 7→ γ), where k = i + 1 is the new position in H30 . Indeed, we have that for any β 0 < µ0 (k) there exists γ 0 with β 0 ≤ γ 0 < µ0 (k) and M, γ 0 6|= ϕ (the inequality can even be made strict). Moreover, the annotation is respected by definition of γ: there cannot be any λ ≥ γ such that M, λ 6|= ϕ. Otherwise we conclude by observing that (M, µ0 ) is a counter-model of one of the first two premises with µ0 = µ + (k 7→ γ) where k is the newly created position. We check that µ0 is monotone, because µ(i) < γ. If γ is a successor ordinal, (M, µ0 ) is a counter-model of the first premise simply because the predecessor of γ invalidates ϕ and the annotation is respected; both hold by construction. If γ is a limit ordinal we have a counter-model (M, µ0 ) of the second premise: we do have that for any β 0 < µ0 (k) there exists γ 0 with β 0 ≤ γ 0 < µ0 (k) that invalidates ϕ, and the annotation is respected by construction. When C 0 ; H2 is not empty, we need to consider whether γ is less than the ordinal to which the positions of C 0 are mapped by µ, and use the last two premises when it is not the case.
